title: LinkedIn AI Slop Is Making Us Worse at Thinking
description: Why synthetic polish spreads on LinkedIn, how it changes what we reward, and a practical way to make AI-assisted writing sound like you again.
coverAlt: An editorial illustration of a glass machine sorting a storm of blank paper cards
lede: The weirdest thing about AI slop on LinkedIn is that it can be perfectly grammatical and still leave you feeling like you read absolutely nothing. That gap between polished and useful is the whole problem.

sources.title: Google Search Central: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content

sections.title: Slop is about effort, not the tool
paragraphs: Calling every AI-assisted sentence slop is lazy. A person can use a language model to organize messy notes, clarify an explanation, or help a non-native speaker write more comfortably. That can make communication better. A carefully edited AI-assisted article can contain more thought than a rushed human one.

The useful distinction is whether the author contributes judgement that changes the result. Does the post contain a concrete observation, evidence, tradeoff, or decision the reader could use? Could the writer defend the central claim if the fluent draft disappeared? If the answer is no, we are looking at text that simulates the shape of thinking without doing much of it.

There is a familiar LinkedIn rhythm: big claim, line breaks engineered for scrolling, a numbered list of easy truths, and a closing question pretending the whole thing happened to you. AI did not invent this voice. It made producing it nearly free. The problem is the production economics: a shape that already performed well can now be made at a volume one person could not previously sustain.
sections.callout: AI is useful as a tool for expression. Slop is the point where polish stops carrying any identifiable judgement.

sections.title: The feed rewards a signal, not a mind
paragraphs: A feed sees a sequence of actions: someone stopped, expanded, reacted, commented, or moved on. It cannot inspect the sincerity of an insight. Platforms describe ranking in terms of signals and relevance, and those signals are imperfect proxies for whether a reader actually learned something. A sharp confession or an incendiary claim may earn activity even when the argument underneath is weak.

That creates a miserable game for people who want to write carefully. A nuanced post takes longer to make, often asks the reader to hold two ideas at once, and may be harder to compress into a clean rule. A generic claim is cheap to produce and easy to recognize. If creators copy the shape of whatever seems to work, the feed gets more uniform and every real observation has to fight through it.

This is not proof that one ranking feature caused the problem. LinkedIn's exact system changes and no public description captures every decision. But the incentive loop is visible enough: creators optimize the signals they can see, and everyone else inherits the texture of that optimization.

sections.title: What brain rot feels like in practice
paragraphs: Brain rot sounds unserious until you notice what repeated low-value content trains you to do. You start skimming for emotional cues instead of following an idea. You mistake a confident opening for an argument. You click, scroll, and remember the format better than the point.

The harm is not that one LinkedIn post permanently damages anyone's brain. That would be a dramatic claim without evidence. The smaller, more believable cost is attention. Every near-empty post asks for a little time and gives very little back. A stream of them can make professional learning feel like checking a feed for status updates rather than encountering people doing work.

And there is a social cost too. If every post reads like a lesson, people stop sharing unfinished questions. They hide uncertainty behind a confident takeaway because vulnerability seems risky and a neat story is easier to reward. That is how a network meant for people to show their work begins looking like a factory for polished conclusions.
sections.callout: The cost is cumulative: less time with the idea, more time with the packaging.

sections.title: A better workflow for AI-assisted posts
paragraphs: Start with material a language model cannot conjure honestly on your behalf: a real decision, a surprising result you actually observed, a failed attempt you can describe, or a question you are still working through. Write that down in plain language before asking for help.

Then use AI for a bounded job. Ask for a clearer outline, missing objections, a list of claims that need sources, or help finding where a reader might get lost. Keep one human draft. Check the references. Remove any statement that sounds like a personal experience you never supplied. Read the final thing out loud. If it would be odd to say in a conversation, rewrite it.

A practical last check is to delete the opening line and see if the body still says anything specific. Then delete the last paragraph. If nothing important disappears, the piece may be mostly hook and moral. That is a reasonable signal to stop polishing and find a more useful observation.
The point is not to prove you never use a tool. The point is to make the post carry your selection of what matters, rather than the model's most statistically familiar version of a LinkedIn essay.
bullets: Name the concrete thing you saw, built, tested, or are uncertain about.
Ask AI for one task at a time, such as structure or counterarguments.
Verify every concrete claim and personal detail before publishing.
Keep the awkward specific detail if it makes the account real.
Cut generic advice that could belong to anyone in any industry.

title: An AI Benchmark Score Is Not a Verdict
description: How to read AI benchmarks without being fooled by a leaderboard. Learn to inspect task design, scoring, baselines, contamination, variance, and the gap between a score and your job.
coverAlt: A paper benchmark score sheet under a magnifying lens
lede: A model can top a benchmark and still be the wrong model for your task. The score is a measurement of a designed test, not a tiny oracle declaring who is smart.

sources.title: HELM: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models

sections.title: What is the test actually measuring?
paragraphs: Before asking which model won, ask what the benchmark authors meant by success. A benchmark operationalizes some construct: coding ability, factual recall, multi-step tool use, speech recognition, or something narrower. It turns that construct into a set of tasks, an interface, and a scoring rule. Those design choices determine what a score can mean.

Suppose an agent benchmark asks models to patch a bug in a repository. Is the score based on exact patch match, tests passing, or a human review? Does each model receive a clean working tree? How many tool calls can it make? A pass can mean the solution is correct, or merely that it passes a small test suite. These are different claims, even if both appear as 70 percent in a chart.

A useful reading starts with the task instructions and the scoring method. Find what counts as a failure. Look at the examples. Ask whether the benchmark's success condition resembles the consequence you care about in real use.
sections.callout: The name of a benchmark is not its methodology. Read the paper or technical report before repeating the headline.

sections.title: Comparisons need the same conditions
paragraphs: A leaderboard invites a simple comparison: system A scored 84, system B scored 79. But was the same model version used? Same prompt budget, search access, retry policy, tools, and inference settings? In agent tasks, the surrounding harness can do a lot of the work. A score belongs to a model-plus-system configuration when those things affect the result.

Pay attention to the baseline. Beating a weak baseline is a weak result. Beating a strong, current baseline under the same conditions is more informative. Check if the benchmark uses multiple runs; stochastic systems vary. A five-point gap across tiny samples can be less convincing than a modest gap that holds across many tasks and seeds.

Even when the report is careful, a vendor headline often keeps the score and drops the test setup. That is where a technically honest result becomes public hype. Restore the context before drawing a conclusion.

rows: What kinds of examples are included?
What exactly counts as a pass?
What tools, prompts and retries were allowed?
How many tasks and repeated runs?
A weak comparator inflates the story

sections.title: A score without uncertainty is incomplete
paragraphs: Many public benchmark tables show one number per system. A single number hides variation across items and, for stochastic models, across runs. Ask for task-level results, confidence intervals where appropriate, or a repeated-run distribution. If the benchmark has a small sample, a slight lead can be noise rather than an advantage.

Accuracy is only one column in a deployment decision. A system that solves more tasks but needs five retries, expensive tools, or a human to inspect every answer can be a worse choice. For speech recognition, word error rate misses whether errors land in names, numbers, or the command that triggers an action. For code, a green test can miss a security regression.

These metrics do not make one universal formula. They remind us to match measurement to harm. The right question is not 'which model is best?' It is 'which system meets the needed quality at a cost, latency, and failure profile we can live with?'
bullets: Read the model version and evaluation date.
Compare systems evaluated with the same prompts and tools.
Look at per-task failures, not only an aggregate average.
Record cost, latency, retries, and human review alongside quality.
Run a small evaluation on your own representative tasks before committing.

sections.title: Turn a leaderboard into a decision
paragraphs: Take the benchmark's best evidence, then translate it into a hypothesis about your workload. If a model improves on repository tasks involving JavaScript issue fixes, you might test it on the actual kinds of bugs in your codebase. The benchmark suggests what is worth checking. It does not complete the check for you.

Build a private set of examples before choosing the system. Include normal cases, edge cases, and a few failures that matter disproportionately. Freeze the inputs and scoring rules so you do not quietly change the test when a favourite model loses. Use blind review for subjective judgements when possible.
That is less exciting than announcing a winner. It is also how you avoid spending weeks building around a number that cannot predict your user's experience.
sections.callout: Benchmarks are useful maps. You still have to look out the window and see where you are.

title: Benchmark Contamination: When Tests Leak
description: What training data leakage means for AI benchmark scores, what contamination can and cannot prove, and how to evaluate models on genuinely fresh work.
coverAlt: A sealed test paper with a small leak of ink tracing the answer
lede: If the exam questions were in the study guide, a high score tells you something different. That does not automatically mean the student cheated. It means the test needs more context.

sources.title: HELM: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models

sections.title: A leak can be accidental and still matter
paragraphs: Public benchmark questions often live in repositories, papers, discussion threads, and model-generated tutorials. A model trained on a large web corpus may see some of that material. Contamination means evaluation examples, or information that gives away their answers, overlap with training data in a way that can affect performance.

The word gets used as an accusation. Overlap is not the same as proof of intentional memorization, and finding a similar string does not establish how, when, or whether the model learned it. But the measurement question remains: if a model can retrieve a familiar solution, is this test measuring generalization to new cases or recall of known examples?
Both kinds of capability can be useful. What fails is presenting a score as evidence of the former when the test may partly reward the latter.
sections.callout: Contamination is a validity problem first. Motive requires separate evidence.

sections.title: Why detecting contamination is difficult
paragraphs: Exact-match searches catch verbatim strings. They miss paraphrases, code that solves the same problem through another route, and materials that were present in pretraining under a transformed form. Conversely, a common phrase or programming idiom can match without meaningful leakage. There is no magic scan that labels every overlap and proves what the model saw.

Evaluators can compare performance on likely exposed examples and newly written examples, vary wording, or construct private test sets after a model checkpoint is fixed. Each method has limits. A new example can still be easy because it follows a known template. A private set can be small or unrepresentative. A prompt change can alter difficulty for reasons unrelated to familiarity.
The right report describes the audit and the residual uncertainty instead of saying 'we checked for contamination' as if that closed the case.

rows: Whether known strings appear in accessible corpora
Whether the model trained on them
How the system handles unseen instances
Whether the test stays private or is broad enough

sections.title: What a credible benchmark report should say
paragraphs: A good evaluation reports the data's origin, cutoff, task construction, and any known overlap checks. It says whether examples are public, whether a model vendor had access to them, and when the test was created relative to the model. It distinguishes data contamination from other kinds of benchmark gaming, such as overfitting prompts through repeated public trials.

For a system used in production, benchmark creators should supplement public results with held-out tasks and ongoing evaluation. Rotate examples carefully. Keep some cases private. Run regression tests when the model changes. Make it possible to see what classes of tasks fail rather than presenting one grand score.

A vendor that will not disclose training data may not be able to rule out overlap definitively. That is a real limit to state. It does not mean every result is worthless. It means claims must be calibrated to the evidence they have.
bullets: Separate evidence of overlap from claims about intent.
Say what contamination checks were actually run.
Use tests written after the model version is fixed when possible.
Keep a private, representative evaluation set for your own workload.
Treat a familiar benchmark as one source of evidence, not the final answer.

sections.title: Designing a more useful fresh test
paragraphs: Start with the behaviour you need rather than a fashionable benchmark. For a coding assistant, collect recent internal bugs after stripping private data, record the intended fix, and define tests that catch the bug without over-specifying the implementation. For a writing helper, score the answer against a checklist created by a person who knows the job.

Freeze a model identifier, system prompt, tools, and retry rules. Run a baseline and a candidate on the same examples. Keep a held-out subset for the final comparison. When a failure appears, add a regression example, but preserve the original test set too so continuous improvement does not turn into a moving goalpost.

You may not know whether a model has ever seen a comparable task. You can know whether it solves your carefully sampled tasks under conditions you can reproduce. That is usually a much better purchasing decision.
